title: Micro-batching
summary: Processing streams as a series of small, frequent batches: the engines that do it, and how to pick an interval that balances latency, cost and file health.

blocks.text: Most 'real-time' analytics pipelines are micro-batch pipelines. Instead of handling each event individually (chapter 20), the engine collects what arrived over a short interval, from seconds to minutes, and processes it as one small batch with batch semantics: one transaction, one commit, one set of output files. For dashboards that refresh every few minutes, this is simpler and cheaper than true streaming.
19.1 What a micro-batch is

blocks.title: One micro-batch cycle
blocks.caption: Recording the input range before processing and the completion after is what makes restart deterministic.

blocks.text: Because each batch has a known input range, a failed batch is simply rerun over the same range. Combined with an idempotent or transactional sink, the result is effectively exactly-once output. End-to-end latency is roughly interval plus processing time plus commit time.
19.2 Spark Structured Streaming
Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded table and runs your query incrementally, by default as micro-batches. The **trigger** decides when batches run:

items: **Default (unspecified)**: start the next batch as soon as the previous one finishes.
**`processingTime='5 minutes'`**: start batches on a fixed interval.

**`availableNow=True`**: process everything available now in one or more batches, then stop. This turns a stream into a cheap scheduled job that still keeps exact progress. It replaces the older `once` trigger.
**Continuous**: experimental low-latency mode with a limited set of operations; rarely used in practice.

blocks.title: PySpark: Kafka to Iceberg bronze every 5 minutes
blocks.text:
raw = (spark.readStream.format('kafka')
       .option('kafka.bootstrap.servers', 'broker:9092')
       .option('subscribe', 'shop.orders')
       .option('startingOffsets', 'earliest')
       .load())

bronze = raw.selectExpr(
    'CAST(key AS STRING) AS msg_key',
    'CAST(value AS STRING) AS payload',
    'topic', 'partition', 'offset', 'timestamp AS kafka_ts')

query = (bronze.writeStream
         .format('iceberg')
         .outputMode('append')
         .trigger(processingTime='5 minutes')
         .option('checkpointLocation', 's3://lake/_checkpoints/bronze_orders')
         .toTable('lake.bronze.orders'))

The **checkpoint location** holds an offsets log (what each batch will read), a commits log (which batches finished) and, for stateful queries, state snapshots. It is tied to the query: changing certain parts of a stateful query makes the checkpoint incompatible. Never share a checkpoint between two queries.

Deleting a checkpoint 'to fix' a stuck stream silently resets progress: the query restarts from `startingOffsets`, producing either a gap or a full replay. Treat checkpoints as production state with backups and change control.

For upserts, `foreachBatch` gives you each micro-batch as a normal DataFrame, so you can deduplicate and run a `MERGE INTO` against an Iceberg or Delta table. Make that function idempotent: Spark may rerun a batch id after a failure.
19.3 Snowpipe and Dynamic Tables
Snowpipe: file-based micro-batches

Snowpipe loads files as they arrive in a stage, triggered by cloud storage event notifications (`AUTO_INGEST`) or a REST call, using serverless compute. It reuses `COPY` semantics, including skipping already-loaded files. Latency is typically around a minute but is not guaranteed. Snowflake's guidance favours files of roughly 100 to 250 MB compressed; very small files raise overhead. Check the current pricing model, which has changed over time.

blocks.title: Snowflake: auto-ingest pipe
blocks.text:
CREATE PIPE raw.orders_pipe
  AUTO_INGEST = TRUE
AS
COPY INTO raw.orders
FROM @raw.orders_stage
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'PARQUET')
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE;
Snowpipe Streaming (chapter 18) skips files entirely and writes rows; use it when the producer is a stream rather than a file writer.
Dynamic Tables: declarative refresh

A **Dynamic Table** is defined by a query and a **target lag**: the maximum staleness you accept relative to its sources. Snowflake schedules refreshes to meet it, incrementally where the query allows, otherwise by full refresh. `TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM` refreshes only when a dependent table needs it, which suits intermediate steps.

blocks.title: Snowflake: a dynamic table with five-minute lag
blocks.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE gold.revenue_by_hour
  TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
AS
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', paid_at) AS hour, country, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM silver.payments
GROUP BY 1, 2;

A low target lag on a large, non-incremental query means frequent full recomputes. Check the refresh mode Snowflake chose and the refresh history before lowering the lag; the cost difference can be an order of magnitude.
19.4 Latency, cost and file size

Every micro-batch pays a fixed overhead: scheduling, metadata reads, a commit, warehouse or cluster wake time. Halving the interval roughly doubles that overhead while data volume per batch halves. On object storage, each batch also writes at least one file per writing task and partition.

Commits per day
Typical effect
rows: Tiny files, heavy metadata growth, constant compute
Near-ideal files, stale for operational use

blocks.text: 19.5 Small files on Iceberg

Each Iceberg commit writes data files, a new manifest, a manifest list and a new metadata file, and adds a snapshot (chapter 22). With a 1-minute interval, 20 writer tasks and 10 touched partitions, a table can gain up to 1,440 x 20 x 10, roughly 290,000 data files per day in the worst case, each a few MB instead of the hundreds of MB that readers prefer (Iceberg's default target file size is 512 MB).

items: Query planning slows as manifests multiply; scans open many files and pay per-request latency on object storage.
Snapshot history grows; metadata files get larger with every commit.
Concurrent writers (a streaming append plus a compaction job) conflict more often at high commit rates.
Fixes: fewer writer tasks per partition, longer intervals, regular `rewrite_data_files` compaction, `expire_snapshots`, and manifest rewrites (chapter 25).

blocks.title: Use case: the five-second ingestion that slowed every query
blocks.text: A team lands sensor data into Iceberg every five seconds 'to be real-time'. After a month, planning a simple query takes longer than running it, and storage request costs rise. Nobody reads the table more often than every few minutes.
items: Interval moved to two minutes; writer parallelism reduced.
Hourly compaction on recent partitions; daily snapshot expiry.
A separate low-latency path (a Kafka consumer feeding an alerting service) kept the second-level use case.

blocks.text: 19.6 Choosing a batch interval

items: Start from the consumer: how stale may the data be when someone or something reads it? Use that, not the source event rate.
Subtract processing and commit time; the interval must leave headroom, or batches queue up and lag grows.
Check file sizes per commit; if they are far below the target, lengthen the interval or reduce parallelism.
Budget compaction and snapshot expiry as part of the pipeline, not as later cleanup.
If a use case truly needs sub-second reaction, serve it from the stream directly and keep the table at a sane interval.

blocks.title: Pick intervals for three consumers
blocks.text: One Kafka topic of e-commerce orders feeds (a) a finance dashboard reviewed hourly, (b) a warehouse-operations screen expected to be under five minutes behind, and (c) a fraud rule that must react within seconds. Propose the engine, trigger or target lag, and table layout for each, and describe the compaction and snapshot-expiry plan for any Iceberg table involved.

items: Micro-batches process small ranges with batch semantics; known input ranges make recovery deterministic.
Spark triggers: default, processing time, availableNow; the checkpoint is production state.
Snowpipe is file-based micro-batching; Dynamic Tables refresh to a target lag.
Each batch pays fixed overhead and creates files and snapshots.
Short intervals on Iceberg cause small files and metadata bloat; plan compaction.
Choose the interval from consumer needs, then verify file sizes and headroom.

blocks.q: What does `trigger(availableNow=True)` do in Spark Structured Streaming?
options: Processes all data available at start, possibly in several batches, then stops
blocks.explain: It drains what is available and exits, keeping exact progress in the checkpoint, so a stream can be run as a scheduled job. It is not continuous mode, and checkpoints are still used.

blocks.q: A stream's checkpoint directory is deleted and the query restarted. What happens?
options: The query restarts from `startingOffsets`, causing a replay or a gap
Spark rebuilds the checkpoint from the sink table
Nothing; offsets are stored in Kafka
blocks.explain: Progress lives in the checkpoint; without it the query begins from its configured starting offsets. Spark does not reconstruct progress from the Iceberg table.

blocks.q: Why does a 10-second commit interval hurt an Iceberg table?
options: Parquet cannot store fewer than 1,000 rows
Each commit adds small files, manifests and a snapshot, slowing planning and scans
Iceberg forbids more than one commit per minute
blocks.explain: There is no commit-rate rule; the cost is accumulation of small files and metadata, which planning and scanning must handle until compaction and expiry run.

blocks.q: What does `TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'` on a Snowflake Dynamic Table specify?
options: The table refreshes exactly every 5 minutes
Queries on it time out after 5 minutes
The table keeps 5 minutes of history
The maximum staleness accepted relative to the sources; Snowflake schedules refreshes to meet it
blocks.explain: Target lag is a freshness goal, not a fixed cron; Snowflake decides when to refresh to stay within it. It says nothing about query timeouts or retention.
